The ancestors of several of my colleagues in this group were from the maritime provinces, and I find them to be industrious and worthy members of the House of Commons.
As one who comes from that part of Manitoba which has suffered from flood conditions, may I say I sympathize with the conditions described by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. I hope the government will continue to do everything possible to look ..after that immediate situation.
I am inclined to agree with the statement -of the hon. member for Souris that it might be necessary and desirable to extend the Prairies Farm Rehabilitation Act so that it would apply to all parts of Canada. That would be a step toward solving the recurring arguments and disputes about jurisdiction, because we would then have one piece of legislation applicable to all parts of Canada, and the matter of jurisdiction would no longer come up.
Recently in Manitoba we suffered severe damage from flooding. In at least two instances the dominion government has a definite share of the responsibility. However I shall not discuss the matter now. There will be an opportunity on another occasion. But if the

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act were revised so as to make it applicable to all parts of Canada I believe we would save ourselves a great deal of time in disputing just where the federal government should take over.
I would leave one further thought in connection with the reclamation of land. Now that immigration is again on the increase, it is particularly important that we look toward possibilities of reclaiming land, whether it be in the east, the west or any other part of Canada, where it is possible. Although this is a large country in area, unfortunately much of the land is not arable. There is a certain amount of submarginal and marginal land which, with the application of certain public works and reclamation projects could be brought under cultivation.
If the Minister of Agriculture is to make good his dream of 15,000,000 people in the prairie provinces, and if he is to find room for a portion of them on the land, I believe it will be necessary to carry out projects in other parts of Canada where land may be reclaimed and put into useful production.
As a member from one of the prairie provinces, I am happy to support the resolution, remembering well that in the years of drought and of other misfortunes the people from other parts of Canada came willingly to our assistance.

speechtext:
May I add my word of appreciation to the minister for having introduced this legislation. I believe it is fitting to put all Canadians behind the maritimers. This is a move in the right direction. As the hon. member for Davenport has said so well on many occasions, Canada as a whole must stand as a whole; all parts of Canada must be behind those in need, and each part must be interested in every other part, so that this magnificent heritage can be kept at its highest possible degree of value and passed on in that condition to the generations to come.
As the hon. member for Dauphin has just said, the reclamation of our soil is extremely important. I am not sure that up to now we have fully realized how precious and sacred our soil is. Anything that tends to destroy it in any part of Canada is a threat to Canada's strength, and must be resisted and overcome.
This brings me to the conditions in the Fraser valley already mentioned. I feel keenly sympathetic toward the people of the Fraser valley because of their great misfortune. It was only a short time ago that my area was in danger of flooding. I would urge upon the government that they take the dollar sign right out of this question of the Fraser valley flooding. In my view the Fraser valley must

be rescued, salvaged and rehabilitated at the earliest possible day, because it is an important part of Canada. The federal government must lead, in collaboration with British Columbia, to put all Canadians behind British Columbia in its time of distress.
If the minister has not already heard, I am sure he will be pleased to know that the St. Mary's river dam, in which he has been so deeply interested, and for the forwarding and building of which he has done so much, has now passed one great crisis. That grand tunnel which had to be constructed in order to divert the water to permit the building of the dam was completed on Saturday, May 22, according to the Lethbridge Herald. That means great rejoicing in my constituency and through southern Alberta. I personally rejoice and I wish to give the minister full credit for his share in this accomplishment.
This helps me to understand how glad members of the maritime provinces must be because of the measure now to be introduced. I wish to assure people from the maritimes that we Albertans and westerners are just as glad as they are.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like other hon. members I am pleased to see the bill is being introduced to reclaim land from the ravages of the sea. I regret exceedingly, however, its limited aspects. It deals with the lands in three provinces, and three only. It is about time Canada realized that there are more than three provinces which may be claimed as being maritime provinces.
British Columbia is a maritime province. Manitoba borders on salt water. So does Ontario; and there will be opportunities in the future, if indeed they do not already exist, when land will have to be protected in all those provinces from the inroads of the sea.
It might not be desirable to include protection of prairie lands in the same bill as protection of marshlands against the sea; but I can tell the minister, who has recently returned from a trip to the Pacific coast, upon which occasion he made certain promises in various parts of British Columbia, that in my constituency there are lands which are spoiled by the inroads of the sea-not through any unusual circumstances, such as the very sad circumstances now being experienced in the Fraser valley, but from the day to day rising of the tide.
There was a few years ago a seawall or dike, if you wish so to describe it, protecting a certain valuable acreage just on the outside of Victoria. It was built not by the early pioneers. not by a benevolent imperial or benevolent French government, but by this government. And when one asks that that dike be continued or be completed for the few remaining feet yet required-and I refer to the locality known as Island-view Beach-we are told there is no money available for the reclamation or for the building of works to prevent the inroads of the sea.
I feel that this measure definitely falls short of much that might be required, in that it limits the ability to spend money for this particular type of work only to the Atlantic seaboard.
As is well known in the house, there has been a tremendous influx of people to the southern part of British Columbia. They need food and any food that can be raised is adjacent to a market. Difficulties have been enhanced recently by the increased freight rates on commodities such as potatoes and other vegetables which must be shipped in. I should like to see the provisions of this legislation extended so that dikes required for the protection of lands on the Pacific coast may also be built. If they cannot be constructed under the bill to be brought in, then I hope the Department of Public Works will complete the dikes which it started, thereby making acreage available for the growing of potatoes and vegetables urgently needed on the coast of British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, I received a letter from home some time ago telling of the tremendous amount of soil that was being carried down the creeks and rivers of Alberta, apparently going into Hudson bay to be deposited so that perhaps some future generations may reclaim it. When this resolution was brought forward here I thought what a shame it was to permit our soils in the western provinces to be lost by erosion, wind and so on and then have to try to reclaim them somewhere else.
Dikes were built in Nova Scotia when the first settlers arrived from France and they are still holding back the sea, while those that have been built since have broken down. Orchards have been flooded, fields ruined and at odd times people have actually been forced to abandon their farms. I know I have harped on this subject many times, but here is a solution of the problem which was offered by a man in 1821. He said:
It appears impossible that the land owners should much longer submit to these intolerable burdens on their estates. They must get ofi these taxes or lose their estates, they must do a great deal more than that indeed, but that they must do at any rate.
I doubt if any finer soil can be found than is the fine silt deposited in these salt marshes.

I have been three times on my feet, Mr. Speaker. On the third reading of the bill I should like to make one or two observations. Many of us are public ownership minded and at the same time we are private enterprise individuals. I do not see anything contradictory in those two positions. Public ownership has done a great deal not only for the province of Ontario but for the dominion and I am in favour of it. At the same time, I am one of those who admire and respect individuals who exercise private enterprise, initiative and industry.
My objection to this particular bill is this. This company went ahead from S75 million to $100 million odd, and then they stepped aside at a time when Canada had to finance a war effort. For that I pay them homage and respect. But when they suddenly jump from $150 million to $500 million, that is rather too much. I woidd have been happier to see them take two bites at the cherry, moving along in an orderly sort of way, so that generations to come could look back and say that they had made steady progress. This sudden jump from $150 million to $500 million is too great to ask of the Canadian people, and in the same sentence may I say that it savours of taking advantage of the investing public, the Canadian people.
The Canadian people during the war subscribed to victory loans and what not and received a substantial return for their money, and now that it is no longer necessary to raise victory loans the Bell Telephone Company find a good open market from those who must of necessity invest funds, namely, life insurance companies and other companies, followed by many private individuals who have to invest some of their funds so that they will not remain dormant.
Bell Telephone Company

Fortunately perhaps for the Bell Telephone Company, they struck a period in Canada's history when interest rates were low. Whether or not they should be privileged, by those of us who are charged with the responsibility of administering Canada's affairs, to step into the money market with very low interest rates, is a matter of concern to the Canadian people. Perhaps I should compliment them on being smart enough to do that. At the same time I think of many persons in Canada who are imbued with the idea of public ownership of public utilities, and they are perhaps distressed to see a great public utility enterprise walking into the market and picking up low interest rate moneys to further their own great enterprise.
I do not for a moment detract from the greatness of the telephone enterprise. They are doing a wonderful job on behalf of Canada, setting an example perhaps for the entire world, since we have more telephones per capita in Canada than any other nation. We are highly privileged to be in Canada and to enjoy this convenience; but let us be honest with the public whom we represent here and say to them:	Yes; this great enterprise has
entered the low money market and taken full advantage of it-too great an advantage of it. They should have crawled a little before starting to gallop. They should have moved up to double what they had before; but when they treble that sum, some of us in this house who are private enterprise men, men who are anxious that our fellowmen should receive the rewards that are due them for their enterprise, initiative and industry, cannot stand by and allow the people to be trampled by big interests. And this savours of big interests.
This bill will pass with reservations on the part of many of us who are convinced that we are not a people who will tamper with public industries that are in need for the benefit of a few. This is a great and necessary public utility; it is expanding, and we want it to expand. There are half a million telephones required and they will make life much easier for our people and raise our standard of living. We appreciate that. At the same time I want hon. members to know that some of us who, so far as private enterprise is concerned, may be called 100 per centers, are convinced that private enterprise, with its initiative and industry, s the best thing that Canada can have, not only in our generation but for many generations to come.
Do not think, Mr. Speaker, that we divorce ourselves from the interests of the ordinary individual and give carte blanche to what the man in the street may call big interests. We

do not want big interests. In fact, "big interests" is a misnomer. I have been privileged to be part and parcel of private enterprise having the objective of improving conditions in Canada and not profiting at all therefrom. While we are privileged to be in a category which handles funds and helps the industry of Canada, at the same time we are thinking of what our duty is to our fellowman in the street. I decry the matter of this increase in capitalization. I am sorry that this organization saw fit to gallop before it started to walk, and to jump away up into this high category. I feel disposed to charge it with taking advantage of a situation which developed through no fault of its own, of this house, or of anyone whatsoever, but as a result of a set of conditions in which you, Mr. Speaker, I, and the rest of the hon. members in this chamber did everything in our power to encourage investment in war loans.
The war is now over. That war bond field is gone. But a great public utility comes in and gets that field while that money is around. That is all right. It is perhaps better that it should be this company rather than some great private enterprise; because in the final analysis, what it is planning to do in its developments will, to my mind, be for the general advantage of Canada; I hope and pray that it will be. Being for the general advantage of Canada, I am ready and willing to sit down and say nothing more about it.
At the same time, on the third reading of this bill, I did not think it should be allowed to pass without some of us who are interested in private enterprise and the development of our great institutions in Canada, criticizing those charged with the responsibility of conducting the affairs of this great enterprise for being just a little bit too hungry at this time, and for being just a little bit too anxious at this time to take advantage of a condition which was not of their own making but which developed on account of a world war tragedy which you, Mr. Speaker, and I have sat in this chamber and studied and talked about during the last decade. They are taking advantage of that world tragedy, in my opinion, to get a maximum of cheap money from the investing public of the Dominion of Canada for the furthering of their enterprise.
I thank God that their enterprise is an enterprise of public utility. If it had not been that, it would have been my privilege to have fought tooth and nail against this legislation from the very inception of it, even though in the same sentence I say to you that I am a private enterprise man. I feel that way about it, never for a moment setting aside in

Private Bills
my own mind the fact that, being a private enterprise man, I am also one of those who believe that public utilities for the general welfare of our fellowman are something that should receive the support of all of us, but at the same time all of us should be left free to develop private enterprise, initiative and industry as it moves forward, as it is bred in the heart and soul of the average Canadian to do, and as you and I like to do.
As to public ownership across the board, I say "No"; but as to public ownership for the great and necessary public utility enterprises,
I say "Of course." Let us have private enterprise for all the possible enterprises there are in this great country of natural resources; and fortunately for you and me, and for our fellow Canadians, there are thousands of them, perhaps scores of thousands of them, ready and waiting for the hand of your sons and mine to develop in this great country of ours.
I will close by saying this. I am sorry that this great public utility enterprise saw fit to grab off from the Canadian economy this tremendous sum of money when perhaps two or three bites of the same cherry might, m the course of a decade, accomplish the same purpose.

I see the incorporators are George Chester Stewart, rancher; Cornelius Jahnke, rancher; Robert Thomas, farmer; Charles Horatio Powlett, rancher and farmer; and that this is to be a body corporate and politic under the name of Canadian Cooperative Processors Limited. This is to be a million-dollar company, but I presume that is not the money of these individuals. I am not quite sure whether it is the money of the province of Saskatchewan, though from what I see in the press from day to day it may be that they are playing around with the money of the province rather than with their own money. However I do not think it is either; I believe it must come from some other group, so that perhaps the sponsor will tell us whence the million dollars will come and to whom the interest will be paid in the final analysis.
[The Acting Speaker.]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I did not quite understand what the hon. gentleman desired when he asked for an explanation. It is true that this appears to be an ordinary share of capital proposition, but as hon. members will see further along in the bill it is not an ordinary joint stock company that is being organized. The shares of SI each will be subscribed as any other shares are subscribed, it is true, but I believe the money will come from various people who deal with the organization. They do not, however, pay money dividends but dividends upon patronage; and the whole setup is of a co-operative nature.

As I say, this is the first time I have seen the bill; perhaps that is my fault. The shares are listed at $1 each; and among other things the company is being formed to purchase or acquire the undertaking carried on by the Horse Co-operative Marketing Association Limited. In the first place, shares at $1 each will not pay for the horses. Then the company is to carry on "the business of producing, collecting, buying, receiving, handling, feeding, slaughtering, processing, transporting, grading, selling, marketing, dealing in, with or without taking title thereto, livestock and livestock products."
This has reference particularly to the handling of horses. From my experience of some thirty or forty years, I should say that today some money may be made in the handling of horses for slaughter, for human consumption. Perhaps thirty thousand of them have gone through hands for which I was responsible during the last three decades, and today I believe some real dividends or returns might be made on an investment of a million dollars. That condition will not last long, however, because I believe the day of the horse is past. In the west I understand that horses are being slaughtered at the rate of two or three hundred a day, and soon they will be all gone. For the benefit of those who may be asked to invest in this company, I say that today, and for perhaps another year or two, your money will return dividends; but these horses are going to be shot, processed for human consumption and shipped to Europe.
*Not long ago I think the hon. member for Swift Current brought us a sample of this horsemeat, to look at or eat if we felt so disposed. I can tell the hon. gentleman that as far back as 1932 I had the pleasure of eating horsemeat in Rotterdam, Holland, so that in common with a few other hon. members I may know something about it. I can remember in my younger days that in one short year I shot ten thousand horses and turned them into pickled beef, the sort of meat that was served at a banquet in Swift Current

Private Bills
not many moons ago. You enjoyed it, too; it was good food. It is good food for our friends in Europe who today are starving. So I say more power to you in the development of this co-operative organization incorporated under this bill. It would be a great thing for Canada to get rid of those horses, which are eating the grass off our cattle ranges. Then we could put cattle in their place.
But that is not my purpose in rising this evening. Just now we are ready for the harvest in making real money out of the slaughter of horses, and for several reasons. First, the people of Europe are hungry. The people of Europe are anxious for beef, meat and food. The people of Europe enjoy eating horsemeat.
As a matter of fact, I remember being in Holland in 1932. The first course we had at our meal was cheese and crackers. Then we had lemon pie; and the last and best course was horsemeat. I had that in Amsterdam. It was served as the last and perhaps the best of the three courses served in a full-course meal.
It is to the general advantage of Canada to get rid of these horses. Perhaps I might take a minute more of the time of the committee, and in doing so I shall make sure that my hon. friend has an opportunity to have his bill passed before the hour expires. In the old days, back in 1925, 1926 or 1927 we let horses run off the range, right up to the far north as far as the Thompson river, and Kamloops. We chased them all down through the foothills of the Rockies and across the border to the state of Montana, I believe it was. Swartz Brothers had planned the slaughtering of
10.000	horses a year south of the border; and these horses traversed the border free of charge. This firm, in turn, slaughtered them and manufactured them into edible horse beef which, in turn, was shipped to Holland. Holland was the central point for the market. Holland sent the horse beef into Belgium and into Germany at prices f.o.b. Rotterdam which were at least ten to twenty per cent higher than prices existing in Rotterdam for ordinary cow beef. In other words, horse beef sold at a premium on the European market over cow beef.
Part of the reason for the premium was this, that quarters of horse beef properly cured and properly taken care of by those who know how to handle horsemeat, and who handle it in a manner similar to that in which we handle moose meat, were placed on the market. Instead of cutting a cross-section of the meat, as you do with beef cattle, you follow down the seam and pull out eight or nine-pound chunks of horsemeat covered by muscular film which encloses those eight or nine pounds, leaving that muscular film around those eight
or nine pounds, and then pickling, curing and packing it, and shipping it to Europe where, in turn, it is smoked in large warehouses in Rotterdam and Amsterdam. You leave that muscular membrane around the eight or nine pounds of shoulder, ham or some other part of the horsemeat, and you find-

speechtext: We are now discussing section 1 of the bill, which deals with incorporation.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and I shall stick religiously to section 1. Before section 1 is the preamble, which prays that this petition be granted. It is a petition pertaining to the persons hereinafter mentioned, and I am referring to those persons hereinafter mentioned. And the persons to whom I am referring are those who are incorporating. These are the persons, sir, who have the great idea that not only will this be for the well-being of the people of Canada, but that it will be for the greater advantage of Canada.
Let me say to the persons who are mentioned in the preamble and in section 1 that I am referring to the product in question, prepared as I have tried to illustrate in what I have said thus far. I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, realizing that I cannot go much farther in discussing that phase of the matter.
Let me add this one sentence, however, that I have seen in scores of farmers' back kitchens in Holland, Belgium and Germany four, five, six, seven, eight or nine-pound chunks of horsemeat, smoked, hanging in those back kitchens. And when the labourer, the breadwinner, went out to work he would have a loaf of rye bread under his arm, and his dear wife would pull down these eight or nine-pound smoked hams.
Probably they were from Canada, but they were shipped from the United States. She would cut off two or three slices; and with those two or three slices, along with that loaf of rye bread, he would go out and work for twelve hours. That is the man who, in the final analysis, will be affected here. These are the men who are praying for this petition in the preamble and in section 1 of the bill. But I wish to warn the committee that the supply of horsemeat in not inexhaustible. The day will come when there will not be as many of these horses available. And I want to warn the committee that that day may be already here, when those who consume this product, in connection with this million-dollar investment, will not want to buy from Canada; and
Private Bills

this, for a very simple reason I should like to state in two or three sentences, namely, that they remember that in 1932 the empire trade pacts were passed, at which time Canada took away from the people in Holland and in Belgium what is commonly known as the pig market, or the meat market adjacent to them in London. At that time the market was given to us in Canada.
Therefore they in turn will buy their horse-meat, and the products I have mentioned, from the United States, in preference to buying it from Canada. That is why the condition is such today, and has been ever since the empire trade agreements.
The petitioners in the preamble to this bill may have great ideas about how much money they will make out of this million-dollar investment-from a province, by the way, which I did not think was asking for outside investments. I think it is our duty to warn them that in the days to come they might not make as much profit out of this venture as they might be making now, when there is a shortage of foodstuffs throughout the world.

I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the sponsor of the bill might have made some explanatory remarks when he was introducing it. I should like to know a little more about it before it passes. Perhaps the questions which have come to my mind as I have read it over for the first time might be easily answered; but I think the sponsor should say a few words about it.
May I ask him why a joint stock company will not suffice for this particular form of organization, and why they have asked for a special act of parliament.
Secondly, I would ask him why the present charter, which I presume is a provincial one, is not adequate for the purposes of this particular organization.
Thirdly, I suggest that either this committee of the whole or some committee to which the bill should be referred ought to go into the matter of how this company is being taxed or is allowed to be free of taxation; because in recent years this particular business which the company carries on has grown to a substantial size.
I shall not discuss the sections of the bill individually, but I would point out that they contain peculiar powers; and I should-

DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE	[DOT]
Production services-Health of animals-
17.	Administration of Animal Contagious Diseases Act, and Meat and Canned Foods Act, $2,611,508.

I am not criticizing this vote, because I know it is necessary, but I want to ask a question which has to do with the estimates generally and which is of importance to the people of Canada. I notice that the amount for temporary assistance is increased by something like 1121,000. That may be necessary; I do not know. Would it not be possible for the Department of Agriculture to submit its monthly payroll to the bureau of statistics, showing the number of employees and the amounts paid for their services, so that the people of Canada would know whether economy was being exercised throughout the service? It would be a check on the spending of the government. As I say, there is an increase of $121,000 for temporary
assistance. Yet the minister was able to get on with less than that during the war. So many of these items for temporary assistance throughout the service are increasing. Session after session I have asked for a return showing the number of employees in the government service and the wages paid monthly. We get them some time after. I wonder if the government has not some system of accounting so that it can keep up to date from month to month. Perhaps reports could come from the bureau of statistics so that the people would know what is going on.

The temporary employees in connection with this vote are largely the part-time veterinarians in the country who are checking cattle for tuberculosis. I think it will be admitted by all hon. members who have been following the discussions that it is the wish of most members of the committee that there should be more rather than fewer of these men. As a matter of fact, we are hiring all we can find and putting them on work that has to be done, and that necessitates higher payments in salaries and expense accounts.

That does not answer the question. I said I was not criticizing. I heard the debate in the house the other night when some hon. gentlemen who know all about this matter asked for more men. What I am asking is that there be a report not only from the minister's department but from all the departments, submitted once a month, showing the number of employees in the various services and also the amount of money paid by way of salaries and wages by the department. That would provide a check on expenditures. I think the public would like to know the numbers. We never hear this until the budget comes on. That is the only time we get the comparison from year to year. When one asks for such returns it usually takes two or three months to get the reply, and that does not seem right to me. With civil servants in the department, a report such as I speak of could be got right out, without trouble, by a well administered department. They ought to have some idea of the monthly payroll if they pay the bills. They must know how many people there are employed. That would provide a check on expenditures from time to time.

Of course, as the. hon. member has intimated, there is a paylist every month and it shows the numbers. It can be taken off that. One of the difficulties in getting returns out in answer to questions is the difficulty I have experienced. A few days ago I brought down a return, which hon. members
Supply-Agriculture

will find in. Hansard, stating the number of employees we have in the Department of Agriculture. It starts back in 1912 or thereabouts. There was a question as to how many we had that year, how many we had, say in 1915, in 1920, in 1930 and so on. Records were not kept in the same way back in 1912 as they are today, and it is difficult to bring down in a short time an answer which is comparable for the different years, though there is no difficulty in bringing it down to the. end of last year or the last month for which the records have been made up. That can be done on short notice, and a statement of the kind that has been suggested is possible, at the end of any month, as to what the paylist is.

I have, these records going back for some time. I always ask for one every year to bring it up to date. But even so, it takes two or three months to get the return. I ask for a return, and it takes two or three months to get it. It would be a good idea to have a return made once a month for all departments. It might come a month late, but it would not involve a great deal of work. You have the payrolls every month and the number of people employed during that month, and it would give some indication as to whether there was economy in the department or not. I am not criticizing the number of people the minister has employed as temporaries, because I do not know enough about the matter. Some members have been asking for more on account of certain tests, and I am not criticizing that, but I say that the public would like to have these statistics month by month.

This vote covers all items under No. 17. I am not rising to express any particular criticism. Rather, I shall try to enunciate an idea which I think will be for the general advantage of Canada. This item for the administration of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act covers the feeding of swine with garbage, does it not? This covers matters relating to hog cholera?
Yes.

Hog cholera in the areas surrounding our cities is, as the minister knows, a serious matter. Herds of from 100 to 1,000 are often wiped out in forty-eight hours or less. During the last thirty years the department has done a good job in the inspection of these feeding establishments. With hogs selling at present-day prices, these feeding establishments are a popular line of endeavour for some of our people to get into, particularly those who have returned from the

last war. I know of three young men, a major, a sergeant and another returned man, who invested their entire savings during the war in a venture of this kind.
The department is doing a good job in the inspection of such premises, the owners of which undertake to feed refuse or garbage from the large centres of population, and I encourage them in this, but I would ask the minister to look up the records and put on Hansard the incidence of hog cholera in the suburban areas surrounding our large cities.
Naturally I am thinking more particularly of the city of Toronto; but I am also thinking of Ottawa, where there is a sizeable industry in the feeding of hogs on garbage collected in the city, and I am also thinking of Calgary. I wish the minister would be good enough to put on the record the incidence of hog cholera in Canada. We go along for four or five or six years with very little hog cholera, and suddenly it breaks out in the maritime provinces or western Canada or Ontario or western Ontario-out Chatham way and Windsor way -and these outbreaks will wipe out the entire investment of hog feeders in different parts of the country.
The feeding of hogs on garbage is for the general advantage of Canada, because the production of hogs by that means is of real magnitude in the output of hog products in the country. I would ask the minister to put on the record the figures in regard to hog cholera outbreaks during the last year, let us say, for the guidance of those who are investing money in the business of which I have spoken.

As my hon. friend knows, those who feed garbage are licensed. The number of licensed feeders across Canada is 579, and the approximate number of hogs fed is 52,750. Of course instructions go out for the cooking of the garbage; and I am informed that if they are carefully followed, and if the feeding lots or pens are kept in the condition required by the regulation and no outside contact is permitted, it is possible to avoid having hog cholera. It has been suggested that I put on the record what has happened in connection with it. How many years back would the hon. member like me to go?
Just a couple.

For 1947 there has been none. There was one outbreak in 1946-47, and forty-four hogs were involved. That was in Ontario. In 1945-46 there was one outbreak in Nova Scotia with 184 hogs involved; there were two outbreaks in Ontario, with forty-four hogs involved. For the three or

four years prior to that, there was a great prevalence of hog cholera. The most difficult year was 1941-42 when there were three outbreaks in Nova Scotia, with 406 hogs involved. In New Brunswick there were three outbreaks, with 186 hogs involved. In Quebec there were nine outbreaks with 1,044 hogs involved. In Ontario, there were fifteen outbreaks with 6,437 hogs involved. In Manitoba there were eleven outbreaks, with 619 hogs involved. There has been none since 1942 in Quebec. There has been none in Saskatchewan since 1940. There has been none in New Brunswick since 1944-45, none in Nova Scotia in 1946 or 1947, and none at all in Canada last year.

I want to thank the minister for the information he has given.
I should like to makes one observation for the benefit of the record. During the last five or six years there has been a great advertising campaign carried on over every radio station to which one listened, with regard to using more soap and more detergents of one kind and another. For the benefit of the minister's department, I am asking it now to do some research work on the question I am about to raise.
In washing down the dishes, thousands of pounds of cleansers of one kind of another and thousands of pounds of soap and alkalis of one kind or another find their way into the garbage can and from the garbage can, after being properly handled, into the systems of these 50,000 hogs. In the days to come, in the next decade, those 50.000 hogs the minister told us about, which are being produced every year, will get more and more doses of alkalis and soaps. I am asking the department to study this problem, to do some research work and to give some advice to these 1,044 hog feeders across Canada in the handling of their garbage before they feed it to the hogs, so that Canada's economy may be implemented by the production of
50,000	hogs from this garbage.
We shall be pleased to have that matter looked into.

In view of the shortage of veterinarians in Canada, what possibilities are there for the utilization of the services of veterinary surgeons who recently arrived in Canada as displaced persons? I understand that a number of them are graduates of various universities in Europe, but that they find it difficult to obtain permission to practise their profession. One of these young men wrote to me and told me that he took this matter up with the provincial authorities in Manitoba and also with the university there,
but was told that, before he would be allowed to practise his profession, he would have to write an examination that the Department of Agriculture in Ottawa prepared. Is that right?
I should also like to ask this question. Most of these young men do not yet speak the English language. Would there be any possibility of arranging an examination in the language which they understand? I do not think these men should be held back if there is a shortage of veterinary surgeons. They do not necessarily have to speak perfect English to understand the cows. I am sure that they could render good service to this country. What procedure could these young men follow in order to be able to find some employment in their particular line?

We have been making some study of the possibility of getting veterinarians from D.P. camps and elsewhere; as a matter of fact, we have made a check on the number that are in the camps, the number who speak English and the number who speak other languages. I quite realize that there are certain sections of western Canada, particularly in the rural areas, where it would probably be an advantage to be able to speak some other language as well as English, or probably even to speak some other language even if unable to speak English.
But that is not the deciding factor. The deciding factor is whether or not the person is a veterinary and has graduated from an institution which is recognized in Canada as being of as high a standard as that of the two institutions we have here. If so, and if they have passed examinations in those institutions which are recognized as being of equal standing with ours, then they have a right to register here and will be dealt with in the same manner as persons coming in from any other country would be dealt with at any other time. Up to now there are none that we know of who have been registered in any of the provinces. But we have been doing something about the matter ourselves with the idea of encouraging them rather than otherwise. We have had these lists, as I say, and we have been negotiating with the associations and otherwise to try to get some of these men out, because we want the work done.

I know two persons who arrived recently. One is a young man and the other is a young girl. Both are graduates of European universities in that profession, and both, of course, do not speak the English language well enough to be able to write an examination. Could these examinations be

arranged in the languages which they speak; and would that have to be done through the colleges or the provincial department of agriculture?

Of course the difficulty in connection with that is largely involved in what the provinces themselves would require. I imagine it would be possible for the western provinces to find persons who could examine these people in their own language. But if that were not possible, then, of course, an examination would require to be conducted in English. The main point upon which the authorities will have to be satisfied is the standing of the university from which these persons received their graduation; and an examination of the courses that are given there I think would make it possible for a qualified person here to determine whether they had been fully instructed. The reason is, of course, obvious, now that there is more money in livestock. The total expenditure on agriculture in this country is far short of what I think it should be. From time to time it has been said of some departments of the government that Canada is doing more than any other country. I want to point out that in the United States the appropriation for agriculture is SI,247 million. We are about one-twelfth the size of the United States; therefore we should devote about $100 million to agriculture. Last year we spent a measly $28 million, and this year it will be something like $41,810,000. I am not advocating that we should spend $100 million on agriculture, but I am suggesting that in some particular cases we should spend more money.
The young farmer who has bought a herd, or the veteran who has bought a herd, and loses it, is not getting a proper compensation at this amount per head. The minister has pointed out that the value of the beef at the present time compensates in this matter. But I would point out that, in respect of the dairy herd, the farmer whose herd goes down is not the seller, because those animals are sent to the slaughterhouse where the packer becomes the buyer and the seller, and the farmer gets just what they give him. In that respect he does not receive proper remuneration for the value of his milk cows. I would urge that this compensation be raised to at least a comparative figure to compensate these people for their loss.

The position is that there has been no inclination to change these amounts as prices go up and down. I must say, however, that the compensation has been higher in the past at times than it is non'. It was higher back about 1918, about the end of the first war when, I presume for the reasons now being stated, prices of cattle were higher.
But we have hesitated to change the amounts up and down any more than is absolutely necessary, because there is always the question as to whether people need more money when the valuations are low than they do when they are high. People who are getting only $20 for the animal perhaps need $100 more, when it is worth only $20 in somebody's market, than they do w'hen they can get $100 for what is left, for what they could sell, in addition to whatever remuneration they could get. Speaking personally, the last animal I

Mr. Chairman, recent
events have brought handicaps to the poultry industry in British Columbia. I crave the indulgence of the committee for a few moments to explain the growth of that industry, the difficulties under which it labours, and to ask the minister if he is prepared to offer any solution, so that confidence may be restored in the industry.
During the past six or seven years the government has encouraged people on the Pacific seaboard to go into the poultry business. There have been representatives from the federal government and representatives from the British food interests urging small farmers to increase their flocks and to construct additional houses.
To give some idea of the enormous growth in the poultry industry as a result of the impetus given by the government, let me point out that, while in 1939 the value of the egg crop in British Columbia was something over $4 million, in 1947 it had increased to almost $16 million.
A few years ago the amount of eggs produced n British Columbia was only one-tenth of chat produced in Ontario. We are now producing one-third and the industry in British Columbia has become second only to that in Ontario. However, in addition to egg production, the production of dressed poultry has increased1 tremendously. I believe last year

something like 12,000,000 pounds of dressed poultry were shipped to Great Britain. I know that even within the last few months carloads of turkeys and dressed chickens have been shipped to points throughout Canada and to the United States. In so far as breeding stock is concerned, shipments of chicks and poults to other parts of Canada have been given a new impetus, as a result really for the first time of the movement of these day-old chicks and poults by air. This remarkable achievement has been accomplished largely through the assistance given by the government.
In 1942 the government offered assistance to the poultrymen of British Columbia by a freight assistance policy. Last year, according to the figures I have, over 100,000 tons of wheat, 33,000 tons of mill feeds and 46,000 tons of barley were sent into British Columbia, on which freight assistance was given. Now we find the ceiling has been removed from the price of that feed grain going to the poultry-men of British Columbia. Before that ceiling was removed, however, the British Columbia poultry industry agreed to sell twenty-five per cent of its entire production of eggs to Great Britain at the definite price of 36}4 cents per dozen for eggs in the spring, this price to increase to 43Yi cents per dozen on September 1. Although the price remains the same, the cost of production has gone up, largely due to the removal of the ceiling price on feed grains.
Not only that, but as everybody knows, in the last few weeks freight rates have been increased; and, as has been pointed out many times in the house, this affects British Columbia particularly because of the unsatisfactory mountain differential. In addition to that, costs of other materials, such as lumber required to go into the construction of breeding pens, houses and the like, have gone up. The result of that is that egg production this year is estimated to drop by something like sixty-six per cent. I believe those were the figures given by Professor Lloyd of the poultry division of the University of British Columbia. The British Columbia poultry industries council have asked that a subsidy be placed upon eggs in order that confidence may be restored. I do not know whether that is possible or whether that is the intention of the government, but I think the minister is aware of the difficulties facing the poultrymen of British Columbia and I would appreciate it if he could indicate what is to be done.

Has the minister taken into consideration the suggestion I made some time ago in regard to setting a price for hogs in the old country market under the British contract? That is important, in that, under the contract as stated by the minister, the price would not be set until some time this November or December. That, I contend, is not good enough, because the maximum price guaranteed for 1949, according to his own words, is only $25 a hundred, and with the production of pork going down as it is across Canada, I think the only hope of increasing production is to get a higher guaranteed price.
I suggested on the former occasion that the price should be set two years in advance, that there be a minimum and maximum price, a floor and a ceiling, and that it be reviewed each year. To give examples, I suggested previously a floor at $30 and a ceiling at $35. That is $5 better than the present floor which is guaranteed for 1949, and I believe the farmers would be satisfied to carry on and increase production on a floor near that. The floor would not necessarily be set at $30, but the price would be within a range of $5 between the floor and the ceiling. That should be for two years, and each year the price could be set at $32 or $33 or $34, somewhere within that range. It would give the farmer a better guarantee. Has the minister taken into consideration anything of that kind, and when will the price be set?

It is not a matter of taking it into consideration. Since 1939 we have been negotiating with the British off and on for many years on these contracts. We did endeavour for some considerable time to have the period increased from one year and were successful in getting it up to two years for a period. We did everything possible last December to have the price set for 1949. There must be two parties to any bargain, and the British absolutely refused to set the price for 1949 any further than to set the floor. I do not know what we can do beyond that. We will negotiate the price as soon as we can persuade the British to sit down with us and discuss it. As a rule, that has been done in the fall, some time after September, and I have some doubts as to whether they will negotiate it before that time this year. It is not a matter of what we want to do; it is a question of what the other parties wish to do in the negotiations.

It is not setting a good example for forward contract prices, and it is not very promising for the next year's price

if Britain has refused to go the two years. She wants to leave it until this fall, and we must suppose the price will be lowered considerably compared with what it was.
Do not suppose too much.

I was looking at the records tonight giving our position and the United States position in regard to hogs. On the barley hog ratio ours has been at 19, and back in the period around the beginning of the war and prior to that it stood at 19 or 20. The United States com hog ratio stood at 17 or 18. Their hog ratio stands at the present time at half that, 9. So that when you take into consideration the cost of feed on the United States side, as compared with the price of hogs, and take the cost of feed on this side of the line as compared with hogs, our position is twice as good as the position in the United States, considering that one factor.

The price of feed is now practically twice as high over there. But the point is this. I do not care where the price is now. It is the price next year that I am interested in. The farmer is not worrying about the price at the moment.
I know.
He is worrying about what the price will be next year.
You are worrying about the same thing that we are worrying about, but the other fellow is worrying too.
He will not get increased production at that maximum price.

He is not asking us to increase it. We have more bacon now to

supply Britain than Britain is prepared to take at the moment. Whether we shall have more in September I do not know.

I would think there would be no difficulty if he is not able to find a market here. I do not think he would have any difficulty in getting an export permit, but he would have to apply to the Department of Trade and Commerce and they in turn would probably refer the matter to us. I have not heard of the case, and I have never heard the question of buckwheat discussed in connection with exports.

Applications have
been made for an export permit, and I was informed that they got in contact with the Department of Agriculture three or four times and were refused as a matter of policy. I cannot understand why, when this man has got in contact with all the milling companies and they are not interested, he should have to lose his car of buckwheat. Here is a letter from the Maple Leaf Milling Company, as one instance. They reply to his letter and say in effect: In reply to your letter of recent date we regret to advise you that we are not in the market for buckwheat at the present time. He has about seven or eight other letters of that kind. Yet the department will not give him an export permit.
Will the hon. member bring that to my attention tomorrow, and I will see what I can do. I do not think there will be any difficulty about that.
Can the minister give us any idea what the price of Ontario soft wheat will be for this season?
That is trade and commerce. I do not like to announce their prices.
Is that entirely under trade and commerce?
Yes.

I have a small matter to discuss. In reading over the order in council quickly, I noticed that in section 4, subsection (d), the board was given the power to report on any questions relating to specific projects for the utilization or control of common rivers or lake systems. Then, under the following section, or a later section, the recommendation of the board with regard to subsections (c) and (d) of section 4 shall become effective when adopted by order in council. When I read that I was of the opinion that, without much stretching of the wording, or that with any reasonable interpretation of that wording, we might perhaps have some system of control of rampaging rivers, at least the ones that are interprovincial. But I think the minister has answered that today by pretty well saying that it is not so. I should like him either to affirm or to disaffirm that.
While I am talking on these matters, I should like to refer to some of the flood conditions in my own riding. I have just returned from a hasty trip up there to look over the flood situation. [DOT] While it is perhaps not on as big a scale as the British Columbia flooding, about which we heard earlier in the day, yet it is a serious matter.
Supply-Agriculture

So far as the Department of Public Works is concerned, on the Assiniboine river, which interests me the most, I must say that on the whole I would not be prepared to criticize what they have done. They have done a reasonable job there and have complied, as far as possible, with the reasonable requests not only of myself but of the members who have previously represented this constituency. There is, however, still more for them to do.
The point I want to talk about today is this. This Assiniboine river rises away up in the Saskatchewan. It is an interprovincial river. Not only that, but the basin of the Assiniboine is a huge one. The Assiniboine river comes down from northeastern Saskatchewan and works in through Manitoba. I think it is joined by the Qu'Appelle before it crosses the Saskatchewan boundary, later by the Souris which is not only interprovincial but also international, and also by the Minne-dosa and other smaller rivers and creeks. From Portage la Prairie on to the Red river, all the water from this tremendous basin, or rather from these basins, has to be funneled through that one river, through which it flows slowly, with a comparatively small drop of about 112 feet from Portage to Winnipeg. The result is that we are faced with these flooding conditions.
It is all very well for the Minister of Public Works to say what he did this afternoon. I have no doubt that he was speaking only upon the opinion of the law officers who advised him. It is all very well for him to say it is not a federal problem at all, but is provincial or municipal. The provincial authorities are equally positive that it is not a provincial matter at all, but that it is a dominion matter. It is cold comfort to the farmers, who have thousands of acres flooded and under water in the Assiniboine basin, to be standing there while two authorities, to both of which they pay taxes, stand aside and attempt to wash their hands of this particular problem. It must be somebody's.
There is lots of water.

Yes, there is lots of water for them to wash their hands. It must be somebody's problem. It is not reasonable to say that the municipality of St. Francois Xavier-which is on the east of my riding, and which takes a terrific beating when there is flooding of the Assiniboine; it is a small municipality of about 48,000 acres-is responsible. It is ridiculous to say that it has any financial responsibility for keeping the Assiniboine river under control, when the Assiniboine river comes from Saskatchewan

and just passes through this small municipality; and the Souris river, which I think rises somewhere south of Regina, not only meanders through Saskatchewan and Manitoba but also, I believe, takes a bend into the United States. As I say, it is ridiculous to say that the municipality of St. Francois Xavier has any responsibility there at all. But somebody has. If it had not been for that diking system that is there now, there would have been half a million acres flooded this year in the municipality which is represented by myself and the hon. member for Macdonald.
Whether the matter is dominion or provincial, 1 do not care, so long as some scheme is evolved. But there should be some authority in this country of ours that will make a survey and develop an over-all scheme. I think it should be the dominion. They should make a survey. Then, if the dominion thinks it is a provincial responsibility or the responsibility of several provinces, the dominion should take the initiative and should not expect the farmers who are flooded to run to the municipality, from the municipality to the provincial government, and from the provincial government to the dominion government. There should be an over-all scheme, and it should be worked out by the dominion.
If the Minister of Public Works is correct, and if the law officers who have advised him are correct, well and good. But if there is a divergence of opinion between the law officers of the dominion and the law officers of the province, I say that in all reason and in all common sense the dominion government should submit the whole question to the supreme court for a decision. Then, if we find out that it is a provincial responsibility, the farmers whom I and others here represent, can go to the proper determined authority to get our relief. As the situation is now, we do not know where to go. We are just pushed around from one authority to another. That is the situation not only in my constituency but in every other constituency that is affected by this flooding. There should be a whole dominion-wide scheme, an over-all scheme of control of these rivers. There should be a survey made of these rivers, and I think these rivers which are interprovincial should be the care of the dominion government without any-I was about to use the expression "passing the buck", but I do not think that is fair to the Minister of Public Works. But I think the P.F.R.A.-and that is under the Minister of Agriculture-should make a survey of the Assiniboine river basin, and of the tributaries of the Assiniboine and

Supply-Agriculture
see just what can be done or what ought to be done in the matter of control by a system of dams, diking or something?
It is just a tragedy that this year some of the best farm lands in the Dominion of Canada are under water to a depth of not only a few inches but several inches. It was just a miracle, and also by reason of the fact that the farmers and the citizens worked together day and night for over two weeks, that half a million acres of the best farm lands in this country were not under water. I do not think it is good enough for the government of the Dominion of Canada or the governments of the provinces to be standing by, each trying to evade whatever responsibility there might be, lest they be handicapped by some responsibility which they do not want to assume, and that they should pass the buck from one to another. This question must be determined at once, even if it is necessary to have a reference to the courts to ascertain whether it is a provincial or a dominion matter.
As far as these estimates are concerned, I suggest to the minister that he give some study to the wording of P.C. 2413, which was tabled today, to see if the intent and wording of the order in council and the agreement attached to it are not wide enough to permit some such survey as I have requested to be made, in an attempt to arrive at a permanent cure for all this flood damage that is being caused.

As to the last matter the hon. gentleman discussed, that is the survey on the Assiniboine river, that survey has been under way for a year and a half. We have already spent $6,000 on it, and we expect it may take another year to complete the survey. But it is being made. One of the proposals is that we put a reservoir in the province of Saskatchewan up near the headwaters of the Assiniboine; and borings are being made there to locate the proper place to put the dam to create the storage in that area necessary to prevent the water from coming down with a rush.
I think one reason that floods have been more prevalent in recent years is the fact that the trees have been pretty well cut in the northern areas. The snows used to go away more slowly when the trees were there, and the water came down more slowly. The trees have now been trimmed off, and the water comes down with a rush. We believe it is possible to correct that condition by building dams and creating storages to let the water come down gradually instead of coming 5849-2884
down with a rush, and that survey is now being made.
It is possible to have surveys of that kind made under this order in council. We were making them before, without the order in council, but this is intended to facilitate that work. The intent of the order is that each province will appoint its chief engineer; we will appoint our chief engineer under P.F.RA.; mines and resources will appoint their chief engineer, and those five men will constitute the board. That board will make a study of the information now available, and we think we have most of the information with respect to water flow and all that sort of thing already on record at the offices in Regina. But if it is not on record, then any one of the provinces or the federal government can ask for further information to be obtained, and it will be obtained by this board. The necessary staffs will be provided; and when we have the complete records with regard to the flow of water in those streams and what might be done with it, recommendations will be made by this board to the governments concerned. It may be that in some cases only the federal government and one provincial government will be concerned, but where all four governments are involved the recommendations will be made to all.
The chief responsibility of the board under this order is to determine how much water we should allow to pass the boundary line from Alberta into Saskatchewan, and how much should be allowed to pass the boundary line from Saskatchewan into Manitoba. It has taken us over a year to have this order in council, as it is now, agreed upon. Last year we had one we thought was satisfactory. We sent it to all three governments and finally persuaded two of them to accept it. The third government, Manitoba, was not prepared to accept it; and perhaps they had some reason for their position. They have muskrat farms in the northern part of the province, which are supplied with water by the big run-off in the spring. In the discussions we took the position that, after all, muskrat farms were not the most important thing; that if we were to control the water in the way suggested by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, namely holding the water back by dams and letting it come down gradually, thus avoiding floods, then the flooding which has taken place in the lower levels may have to take place higher up, for the time being, and the muskrats would have to go up there and have their homes.
Some of those things, I think, will have to give way to the development of the larger idea, that idea being that there is not enough
Supply-Agriculture

water, and that we should not allow it to rush away to Hudson bay in the spring, but should provide storages all back along the route wherever they can be usefully placed, and that we should permit the same amount of water to go through in the twelve-month period, but that it would be spread over the year instead of all going down in two or three months and then there being none at all for another period. That is the idea behind it, and this board is set up for the purpose of recommending to the provincial governments and ourselves what should be done.
After those recommendations come in, it is assumed that the federal government will provide the money for the storages. We do not undertake to provide the money to put in irrigation or to put in power developments, but we undertake to provide money for storages. Once we have decided that a storage can be utilized effectively either by a province or by some local organization which has been set up, or by the municipalities, then we may undertake to build that storage.
Or for the purpose of controlling floods?

Well, I would say it will serve the two purposes at the one time. In most cases it will be to provide power or to provide water for irrigation. For example, if they create a lake on the Saskatchewan river by building a 200-foot dam, that lake will be 145 miles long. It will be 200 feet deep at the dam and some fifty-three feet deep north of Swift Current.
Is it not the intention of the dominion government to expend some sixty-five or sixty-seven million dollars, provided that this dam proves feasible?

I am not sure it will spend $66 million. It will spend whatever part of $66 million is necessary if it is once determined to go ahead with the program, and if we have the consent of all the provinces to go ahead with it.
Then may I ask this question?
Not too many questions at once.
I think I had the floor.
But I was answering a question asked1 by another hon. member.
Any single province has the power of veto on this, has it not?

Not now. The order previously drafted provided that any one province would have the power of veto, but that is not this order. That previous order was not signed; it has been changed. The present order does not provide that this board shall make any decisions. It simply makes a recommendation to each province. We did not want it that way, but that was insisted upon by the three provinces. We finally agreed in order to get somewhere. We were a year trying to get them to agree to the other proposal, that the board should make the decision in the matter, but they do not want that. We have agreed to allow recommendations to go to each province and to us; but we are trusting that the provinces will pass the necessary orders in council, when the time comes, in order to make it possible to proceed.

Then each province still
has a veto?
No such thing as a veto is involved, but if they do not pass an order in council nothing will be done.
In effect, then, they can block it?
Yes.
Did I understand the minister to say that the dam to be erected somewhere near Elbow will raise the water at Swift Current or at Saskatchewan Landing to a height of sixty-six feet?

No; fifty-three feet. I understand that if a 210 foot darn is built at Elbow, which is the one recommended by the engineers, that will necessitate building a dam 110 feet high along the east side of the Saskatchewan river to prevent the water from going down the Qu'Appelle. Both those dams would have to be built before you could have that supply of water provided in the Saskatchewan river; and I imagine the water would be 200 feet deep at the dam.

The minister did not get my question. He says the dam to be erected somewhere near Elbow will be 200 feet high.
I understood him to say that would raise the water in the vicinity of Saskatchewan Landing north of Swift Current to a depth of about sixty feet.
To fifty-three feet.
One further question; that would wipe out the possibility of a low-level bridge being erected there.

I understand that what they are proposing to do now is to put in the

Supply-Agriculture
abutments for a 53-foot bridge, but to build the low-level bridge. That is the situation at the present time, so far as I know it. A 14-foot increase in water would result from a different dam altogether from the one at Elbow. There have been a number of investigations made, and if a dam different from the Elbow dam were built, then it might be possible that the lake would only create an increase in water level of fourteen feet. I understand that the province intends to go ahead and put in abutments which will carry the high-level bridge. But they intend at the present time to build a low-level bridge.
The advice that they have and that we have is that the steel structure put on the low level can be jacked up to the higher level, and the full abutments are built to carry that higher level bridge, if it is ever necessary in the future. Then they would have to add approaches at both sides back to the higher level of the river banks.
The suggestion was made a while ago to build another dam at Saskatchewan Landing, which would mean a lower dam at Riverhurst or Elbow, and then, have that new dam at Saskatchewan Landing.

There is only one dam being discussed at the present time, and that is the 210-foot dam at Elbow, which would necessitate a second dam on the east side, because the bank of the river opposite the Qu'Appelle is only ninety feet high. If you build a dam 210 feet high, you have to build another dam along the east side of the river to prevent all the water from going down and flooding out all the people in Manitoba. So there has to be a great deal of construction. The plan has been suggested which will take a considerable amount of money, if proceeded with, and some time to build.
Has the minister anything to indicate from his records where the proposed dam would be on the Assiniboine river?
They have not completed the borings. But it is somewhere up in the Saskatchewan area, in the vicinity of Kam-sack.
It would have to be above the Minnedosa and the Souris.
Yes.

I have a number of questions I should like to ask, which certainly do come under this item. First, may I remind the minister that during the past few years I have been quiet and considerate in asking for any information concerning the matter I have in mind. But, after the tremendous snowfall we had during the past winter, and the tremendous amount of run-off water, I should like to inquire from the minister as to how much water is impounded in Wolverine creek by the dam built by P.F.R.A. southeast of Humboldt in the summer of 1943. Have any repairs been made to this dam in the past year, and, if so, what was the total cost of such repairs?
The dam at Wolverine creek is really an underground dam.
That is a new kind of dam.
An election dam.

No, it is a sensible kind of dam. The underground structure is of gravel and no better water in the world can be had than that stored in gravel. Steel piling is driven down at the end of the area in which the water is stored. The run-off in the spring soaks into that and is stored. A total of $479.75 was spent last year on repairs.
For what purpose?

I am not sure of the purpose, but I presume it had something to do with the structure. I imagine my hon.

Supply-Agriculture_____________
friend knows more about it than I do, because he lives close to it.

My information is that a wooden overflow structure was burned by a prairie fire. I do not know just to what extent the department has repaired it, but in repairing it I hope they see that this dam which is supposed to hold water will not be consumed by a prairie fire.
Firewater.

I should like to find out how much water is now impounded by this dam. Last year and the year before, I made special trips out to the dam, one time right after there had been a cloudburst in Humboldt which had raised the level in Burton lake near my farm to about ten feet. When I got to the dam there was not enough water to permit a respectable duck to take a bath. I want to know whether this dam is going to hold any water at any time.
I think if my hon. friend took a jump down one of the wells down there he would find that there is more water in it than there ever was before.
I hope the minister is not suggesting that I go down a well?

It was never intended to be a duck pond. It is on the same principle as that by which water is supplied to Moose Jaw. Water comes down from the Saskatchewan river seventy miles away, it is pumped into the sands, and then Moose Jaw pumps it out again and takes it eighteen miles into the city. This dam is some six or seven miles from Humboldt and there is a graveled underground area in which water is supposed to be stored. So far as I know, Humboldt has never attempted to pump water out of it and, until they do, they will not know whether there is any water there. I presume there is water there because the dam is properly constructed.

The town of Humboldt and their advisers in the matter of water supply have been hesitant to undertake the placing of a pipeline to that dam, because until this spring there has not been sufficient water to warrant the expense. The minister's statement that this dam was constructed with the idea of checking the flow of water underneath the surface is understandable-
Is correct.

Then why was it necessary to construct a dam forty or fifty feet in height if it was intended to hold water flowing underneath the ground? The engineers of the
department must have had some idea that sufficient water would back up behind the so-called underground dam to raise water on the surface against the dam. The minister or his officials can find out much easier than I what water is impounded by this dam. There was a tremendous amount of run-off water this spring.
Both the hon. member and I will be out there before very long and we can look at it.

I hope the minister will so arrange his trip that I can have the pleasure of driving him to that dam. I assure him that I will not invite him to jump in a well because I know we can get along very well without that.

None under P.F.R.A. on construction. The money that is being spent in British Columbia is being provided from two sources. One is the Veterans Land Act. A considerable amount of work is being done under that act in different parts of British Columbia and our engineers are doing the work. In view of the minister's earlier remarks that the. cause of all this flooding we have had is the destruction of forest cover to the north, I have a question to ask which has a particular bearing upon northern Ontario. What steps, if any, are being taken to replace the forest cover?
All the work being done to replace forests I presume is done by the provinces because the forests belong to the provinces.

If one province refuses to adopt the recommendation of the water board with respect to the allocation of waters of a specific river, are we to understand that all development of water storage will be held up until such time as the recommendation is adopted?

We are spending the money and that is exactly the point of view I took with the provinces. I said, "If you are going to delay expenditures I do not think anyone here is going to insist that we spend money in the province". This is doing work

which, according to the discussions we have been having, is really the constitutional responsibility of the province. We are prepared to drop that and do the job up to a point. So far as we are concerned in this department, we have our troubles in getting money. We have to discuss the matter with the Minister of Finance, with the whole council and with all those who are interested in the matter. We have our own difficulties the same as any department has in getting the amount of money which we think ought to be expended. If the provinces are going to say, "We do not want it expended," that will make it more difficult. But I think you will find as you go along that the provinces will expedite it. I do not think there is any occasion for setting up hypothetical cases and saying they will not.

Has the minister had any communication with Manitoba with regard to work being done in the southeastern part of that province? The minister will recall that last year and the year before, I pointed out that there was a great deal of work to be done in the southeast corner of the province, east of the Red river. This area has two or three very large swamps which overflow every spring. There are only two small rivers, the Rat and the Roseau, to take the water away and their banks are not high enough to take care of the flow, so that there is an overflow over the country generally every spring, which makes it very difficult for people to settle there. They have to restrict their settlement to the higher places.
In the past the argument brought forward by officials of P.F.R.A. was that it was more a problem of drainage than irrigation. However, an engineer has come out with the suggestion that probably one storage dam located somewhere on the Roseau about the centre of the area would hold back the main waters from the swamp, and the rivers would then be able to take care of the rest of the drainage. There are several thousand acres that could be settled and cultivated and put to real use in that area with proper drainage. I commend this project to the minister. I was given to understand that he had discussed it on many occasions with the officials. Is the minister in a position to make a statement on that?

The present situation is that the area east of the Red river in Manitoba is in much the same position as all other parts of Canada outside the P.F.R.A. area, which is the Palliser triangle, and the area east of the Red river is not in that triangle.

I was referring to the eastern side of the Red river but only to the extent

of five or six townships east of the Red river. As I understand the present regulations, most of this area would come under P.F.R.A. because it includes the water basin of the Red river, and the area I am speaking of is part of the water basin of the Red river. I was given to understand that by the official.

If it is in the P.F.R.A. area, of which I have some doubts, it would come under P.F.R.A.; but, if not, it would have to come under another item which provides a special fund for doing works in different parts of Canada.
I am satisfied that it comes under P.F.R.A.
If so, it could be considered.
Has the minister had any communication from the province about it?
Not that I recall.

I should like to bring up a matter which seriously affects Dauphin constituency. I assure the minister that it will not require any subterranean dams or anything of that kind. The minister will recall that about a year ago-

My question was in regard to the marketing of cheese. Is it the intention to requisition cheese for overseas shipment this year? We were interested in the announcement the minister made this afternoon concerning that other great dairy product, butter. It appears doubtful whether this country will have enough butter next winter, with the low price announced today, which I think will have a tendency to discourage production. We have to bear in mind that our population is increasing in this country, and it is questionable whether we can go on exporting dairy products fox any length of time and still have enough left for the home market. We know the tremendous shortage of butter that we experienced last winter and the great demand by consumers for a subsidy. I would hope that the policy of the government will not lead us into that position another year. At

Supply-Agriculture
least the ceiling should be taken off butter at the present time. Would the minister make a statement on that?

With regard to cheese, the price in the contract is thirty cents. It sets a floor under cheese. The requisitioning of cheese depends on two or three things. One is whether we can buy cheese from week to week as we go along in order to fill the British contract. Another one is whether we shall be able to get funds to be able to pay for all the cheese in the month or two toward the end of the season. In my opinion we ought to be able to get our proportion of the cheese every week during the summer, and I have expressed that opinion to the cheese producers in the last two or three days. They are discussing that matter with the possibility of bringing it about, so far as the cheese producers of Quebec and Ontario are concerned.
I am not in a position to say anything more until those discussions are completed. It is not our desire to requisition cheese, and I hope we shall not have to do so. We hope to get the cheese as we go along, rather than have to take it in the last month or two. I think that is advisable. Nor do the British want it all in the last month or two, but week by week, and that is the way we ought to deliver it. But if we cannot deliver it in that way we shall have to make some different arrangements from what we have now.
We have not lowered the ceiling on butter. We have simply said that if it goes down to fifty-eight cents we are prepared to buy it. But butter has not gone down to fifty-eight cents, and I do not know whether it will or not. We have not lowered the ceiling. It is still sixty-seven cents. The papers said seventy-three cents, but there is no such ceiling on butter. The ceiling is a wholesale ceiling of sixty-seven cents, and the fifty-eight cents is in relation to sixty-seven cents, and not in relation to seventy-three cents. The selling price, as everyone knows, is sixty-seven cents, basis Montreal, and the price at which we shall buy, if it goes down to that, is fifty-eight cents.
Does the minister think we shall get enough butter to supply the consumer demand next winter at that price?

I am not sure that it will go down to that price. The price today is sixty-three cents. It has gone down from sixty-seven to sixty-three cents within the last three or four days. Whether it will go lower I do not know, but we are hopeful that butter will come in at these prices. As a matter of fact, the greater part of the surplus butter
comes from places where cheese is not produced.
